subject: Critical Thinking
title: Logic and Language: When Words Deceive
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Logic and Language: When Words Deceive.

hook.text: 'Nothing is better than happiness. A sandwich is better than nothing. Therefore a sandwich beats happiness.'

buildup.text: Natural language is ambiguous. 'Nothing' means different things in each premise. Logic exposes the trick.

discovery.text: Politicians exploit this constantly: vague words that seem logical but fall apart under formal analysis.

twist.text: Even 'and' and 'or' cause trouble. In law, 'or' is exclusive; in everyday speech, it's often inclusive.

climax.text: Translating natural language into logic reveals hidden ambiguity, assumptions, and fallacies.

punchline.text: Language persuades. Logic clarifies. You need both.

quiz.question: Why does the 'sandwich vs. happiness' argument fail?
options: The word 'nothing' changes meaning between premises

details.summary: Natural language is full of ambiguity, vagueness, and hidden assumptions that can make invalid arguments appear valid. Understanding how language obscures logic is essential for critical evaluation of everyday arguments.
details.whyItMatters: Most persuasion happens through language, and logical errors hidden in ambiguous wording are among the hardest to detect.
takeaways: Ambiguity allows equivocation between different meanings
Vagueness creates false precision in arguments
Translating arguments into explicit logical form exposes hidden flaws

faq.question: How does linguistic ambiguity create logical errors?
faq.answer: A word used with two different meanings in the same argument can make an invalid argument look valid. This equivocation fallacy is extremely common in everyday debate.

faq.question: What is the best defense against language-based reasoning errors?
faq.answer: Paraphrase arguments in precise, unambiguous terms. If an argument falls apart when you clarify the definitions, the original version was trading on confusion rather than logic.
